Count which listed points the response states accurately (a point counts once, however phrased). Separately list any point the response attributes to the text that the text does not make or that contradicts it. Reply with JSON only: {"recalled": [point numbers], "inaccurate": ["..."]}

1. A claim's weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it
2. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight
3. Ask who has examined a claim and how closely; long-time colleagues' conclusions have been tested in ways not visible on the page

5. A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it

7. Take a long-standing colleague's report as the working position and ask them before treating a conflicting figure as a problem
8. Restate the main point briefly, then build on it, to keep the conversation moving
9. Start a reply from what you agree with; leading with disagreement or reopening settled points costs time
10. If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask
11. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source; go to primary material only if none exists or someone asks
12. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and signals distrust; private readings fragment the team

15. Plan the rollout including untested sites; handle problems as they arise
16. Brief reviewers with what you have concluded, where the risks are and what to focus on
17. As a new reader, start from what others have concluded
18. Raise objections only when well-founded and the moment is right, privately and once you are sure

RESPONSE:
These are from memory. Most are close paraphrases; the short phrases in quotation marks are the ones I'm fairly confident were the note's own words.

## Framing
- Title: "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It is about working with the team's material and with the people around you.
- It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned
- Every claim has earned a certain weight, whether it comes from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes.
- Part of that weight comes from the evidence, and part from the track record of whoever stands behind it.
- Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask of each claim who has examined it, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues with years in an area have usually been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence "is itself evidence," because it reflects checks they have already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common.
  - Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected by others.
  - Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- **Example:** a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports that its defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position. If a later figure seems to disagree, ask them before treating it as a problem.

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer
- Before responding to a paper, message or review, take it in and show that you have.
- Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it.
- This is not politeness; it keeps a conversation moving forward rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find what's right, say so, and extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement put people on the defensive and cost more time than they save.
- If something is unclear, it is usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- "A restatement is the ground, not the contribution." The useful reply is the next step the shared understanding makes available.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. The reply confirms the overall direction, picks up the points you can act on now, and says the budget will follow in due course.

## 3. Go to the source
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source.
- Go back to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal that you don't trust colleagues.
- A shared record lets the team build together without each member reconstructing it alone.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into "private versions of the truth" and stops being able to act.
- **Example:** a report is summarised as "costs fell 12%." Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you are quoting *the summary* accurately.

## 4. Do not leave open what can be closed
- Some questions the evidence settles and some it leaves less certain. Mark which is which, then keep the work moving.
- An open question has costs: it blocks decisions, invites repeated discussion, and leaves colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on.
- A working answer can be revisited if something new comes up; "a question left hanging tends to stay hanging."
- The mirror failure is more common in careful people: keeping a question open because one more check feels safer wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed and save energy for questions that are still live.
- **Example:** a trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Handle problems there as they arise.

## 5. Help the colleague who sees differently
- New colleagues, and those from other parts of the organisation, often see material differently. That is valuable only if their time goes where it is useful.
- A reviewer who starts from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team already knows.
- So prepare them: tell them what you have concluded, where you think the risks are, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster.
- In reverse, when you are the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they are well-founded and the moment is right.
- A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you are sure of it.

## 6. Make your moves where they will land well
- You will often see a good next step. Before taking it, check that it fits what the owners of the area have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating them, make the call once the direction is confirmed, and release the result when it is ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone, which costs more than a short conversation beforehand.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position; the owner can see considerations you can't.
- Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not a licence to wait indefinitely. Small, routine steps don't need sign-off, but for steps that affect others the default is to check first and then act together.
- **Example:** rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether they would like it restructured, and how.

## 7. Failures come in pairs
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one tends to push you toward the other.
- **Overclaiming / second-guessing:** overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
- **Inventing a flaw / overlooking one:** finding a problem that isn't there in order to look rigorous; missing one that is.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long:** declaring a question answered before it is; refusing to accept the answer the team has reached.
- **Abandoning a line / relitigating one:** dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening one the team has already decided.
- **Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively:** accepting anything said; disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
- **Acting alone / waiting too long:** making calls others should have shaped; delaying steps that have already been agreed.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check that you haven't landed on the other.
- "When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one."

## A last word
- This is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team itself: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, and a direction everyone has agreed.
- "Trust those. They are how good work gets done together."
